title: Handling Holy Offerings with Care
overview: This chapter sets rules for who may eat the food offered at the sanctuary and what kinds of animals may be offered, all to keep the LORD's holy name from being treated lightly.

parts.label: Priests who are unclean (vv. 1-9)
parts.note: A priest who became ritually unfit, through a skin disease, a bodily discharge, or touching something like a corpse, could not eat the offerings that fed his family until he was cleansed; lighter cases ended with a bath at sundown. Being unclean was not the same as sinning, but ignoring the rule was treated as contempt, and scholars are unsure whether being 'cut off' meant exclusion from the community or death.

parts.label: Who may eat the offerings (vv. 10-16)
parts.note: The priest's share was for his permanent household, so guests and hired workers could not eat it, while enslaved people he owned or who were born in his house could. A daughter who married outside the priestly families lost this right but regained it if she came home widowed or divorced with no children, and anyone who ate by mistake had to repay the value plus a fifth.

parts.label: Animals without defects (vv. 17-25)
parts.note: Animals offered had to be healthy and whole, not blind, injured, diseased or castrated, though a slightly misshapen one could be given as a voluntary gift but not to pay off a vow. The chapter does not say why; some readers compare it to bringing a proper gift to a king, and Christians later read the flawless animal as a picture of Jesus.

parts.label: Newborns and their mothers (vv. 26-30)
parts.note: A newborn animal had to stay with its mother for seven days, and a mother and her young could not be killed on the same day; many readers see gentleness here, though no reason is given. A thank offering, a meal shared to celebrate gratitude, had to be eaten the same day.

parts.label: Why it all matters (vv. 31-33)
parts.note: The chapter ties every rule to one point: the LORD is holy, and he is the one who brought Israel out of Egypt to be their God. Keeping these rules was a way of honoring his name instead of treating it lightly.

think: When something matters deeply to you, how do you tell the difference between giving it real care and simply going through the motions?
